annotations.title: Rank which inputs drive an outcome most (one-at-a-time sensitivity)

description: Ranks a model's uncertain inputs by how much each one moves a chosen outcome, and returns the data for a tornado chart (a bar chart with one horizontal bar per input, the biggest swing at the top). This is a one-at-a-time (OAT) sensitivity analysis: it shows how much the outcome changes when each input changes on its own. Every input is held at its median while one input at a time is set to low, middle and high values from its own distribution (by default its 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles). The tool records how the outcome's average changes. Use this when you need to know which assumption matters most, so you know what to research or de-risk first. It returns one entry per input, ranked so rank 1 has the biggest impact. Each entry lists the input values tried, the outcome at each, and an elasticity score. Elasticity is about how many percent the outcome's average moves when the input moves 1 percent, averaged over the values tried. It is never negative: it says how much an input matters, not which way it pushes the outcome; to see the direction, compare the outcome at the input's low and high values. It returns numbers, not an image. Inputs whose distribution produces a list of values are skipped. It takes the model inline in graph, or a saved model by graph_id, so call it directly when the user asks about a saved model, even one that may be unfinished: if an input has no distribution yet, the call is refused with incomplete_model, which names every such input and costs nothing, so the refusal itself tells you what to fix. An analysis that starts returns a run_id. It runs the model once per input per value tried, so on a big model it can take minutes: if it is not done in about 40 seconds (150 seconds without an account) you get status running, and get_simulation_results gives you progress and then the ranking. Cost: it counts as one run per call, however many times it runs the model inside, and it is charged only if the analysis succeeds. Without an account, 1 of your 3 free runs per UTC day, for a model up to 1,000 trials and 20 nodes; that daily allowance is counted per network address and client, so on a shared platform such as Claude.ai or ChatGPT you may find today's free runs already spent by someone else. Signed in with a free Kromatic account, 1 of 10 free runs per UTC day, for a small model (trials x nodes x periods at most 100,000, and within 10,000 trials and 50 nodes), spent before any credits. Beyond that, 1 credit for a small model or 5 for a large one (a large model is any model over 100,000 trials x nodes x periods), currently $0.50 per credit; buy_credits tops up. A model that is invalid, or over the limits of the tier you are in, is rejected before running and costs nothing, and so is a saved graph refused with incomplete_model: no credit, no free run, no run recorded. An analysis that starts and then fails partway through is refunded only where something can be given back: credits are not charged, and a signed-in free run goes back into today's allowance, but a free run without an account is not refunded and stays counted for the day.

detail.description: How much to return. summary (the default): one row per input with its rank, its low and high values, the outcome at each, the swing between them and its elasticity. full: also each input's whole response curve.
detail.title: Detail

graph.description: The model: root_nodes (uncertain inputs), calc_nodes (formulas), edges (links; formulas refer to them like {e1}) and run_params (trials and time periods). Same format as run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph, which documents formulas, periods, distributions and financial metrics in full. Give this or graph_id, not both. Only this outline is published here: the full schema is on run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph parameter, and the neumann://catalog resource lists every distribution and formula function. Neumann checks the model against that full schema when you call this tool and names any problem.

graph_id.description: The id of a graph you already saved, to analyse that graph instead of sending it inline. Give this or graph, not both. Requires a Neumann account -- an anonymous caller must use graph instead. If an input in the saved graph has no distribution yet, the call is refused with incomplete_model, which lists those inputs. The refusal costs nothing (no credit or free run is spent and no run is recorded), so there is no need to check your balance: give each one a distribution, save the graph again under the same id, and try again.
graph_id.title: Graph Id

num_quantiles.description: Instead of quantiles: how many points to try, an even whole number from 2 to 10. That many percentiles are spread evenly between the 5th and 95th, and the median (0.5) is added. 2 gives [0.05, 0.5, 0.95]; 4 gives [0.05, 0.275, 0.5, 0.725, 0.95].
num_quantiles.title: Num Quantiles

quantiles.description: A list of points in each input's own distribution to try. Each point is a fraction from 0 to 1 naming a percentile: 0.05 is the 5th percentile, the value 5% of outcomes fall below. Default [0.05, 0.5, 0.95]. Give this or num_quantiles, not both.
quantiles.title: Quantiles

seed.description: Optional whole number that fixes the random draws, so repeating the call gives the same result. Exact repeats are guaranteed only for small runs, where trials × nodes × time periods is at most 100,000.
seed.title: Seed

target_node_id.description: The id of the outcome node to measure. Defaults to the last calc node in the model, which is usually the final outcome.
target_node_id.title: Target Node Id

time_period.description: Index of the time period to measure, counting from 0: with 12 monthly periods, 11 is month 12. Defaults to the last period. This measures the node's value in that one period, not a total. For a cumulative figure such as year-one profit, add a running-total calc node with formula {e1} + {e2}, where e1 brings in the per-period value and e2 is an edge from the running-total node to itself with delay 1. Then target that node at index 11. This delayed self-edge is allowed; only loops with no delay are errors. In run_monte_carlo_simulation, use a cumsum metric instead.
time_period.title: Time Period
